title: Safety Shot Review: Does It Really Lower Your BAC?
excerpt: An honest Safety Shot review: what's in the drink sold as lowering blood alcohol, what the science says about sobering up faster, and why you should never drive on it.
metaDescription: Honest Safety Shot review: does the drink really lower your BAC? What's in it, what the science says, pros and cons, and why you should never drive on it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest verdict first:** Safety Shot is a canned or bottled drink that has been marketed with a bold promise: that it can lower your blood alcohol content (BAC) faster than your body would on its own. That claim is the whole reason most people search for it, and it is also the part you should trust least. We could not find an independent, peer-reviewed trial showing that Safety Shot meaningfully lowers BAC in real drinkers. The company has pointed to its own testing, but company-run studies that haven't been published in full for outside scientists to check are not the same as proof. Even if a drink did shave a little off your BAC, it would not make you safe to drive. **Never use Safety Shot, or any drink, as a reason to get behind the wheel.**

**Who it might suit:** someone curious about a vitamin-and-electrolyte drink after a night out who has already arranged a ride home and treats it as a recovery beverage, not a sobering tool. **Who should skip it:** anyone hoping it will let them drive, pass a breath test, or "reset" before work, and anyone who wants a product backed by independent research.

> **This is not medical or legal advice.** This review explains the company's public marketing, general press coverage, and the well-established science of how your body clears alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor, pharmacist, or lawyer. **No drink, pill, or shot makes it safe to drive after drinking.** If you have been drinking, use a rideshare, a taxi, public transit, or a sober friend. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning, such as confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, pale or bluish skin, seizures, or can't be woken up, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away and don't leave them alone.

**About our relationship with Safety Shot:** we have no affiliate arrangement with Safety Shot, so this review does not link to its store and we earn nothing if you buy it. We do earn a commission on two DHM products mentioned near the end, and we say so where they appear.

## What Safety Shot Is

Safety Shot is a beverage made by a small US company that trades publicly under the same name (it was previously known as Jupiter Wellness). The product launched with heavy marketing around one idea: that it was the first patented drink designed to help your body lower blood alcohol content quickly. That pitch got a lot of attention, partly because it promised something no mainstream health authority says is possible in any meaningful way.

The company has changed its branding, packaging, and messaging over time, so the product you find online or in a store may be labeled or described differently from older ads and news stories. That matters for this review: we can only assess the general idea and the publicly stated ingredients, not a specific batch you might buy today. Always read the current label.

### What's in it

Based on the company's own descriptions, Safety Shot is a blend of ingredients you'll recognize from many recovery and wellness drinks:

- **Vitamins**, particularly B vitamins and vitamin C.
- **Electrolytes and minerals**, the salts that help your body hold onto fluid.
- **Amino acids and other "metabolic support" ingredients.**
- **Sugars**, which matter more than they sound (more on that below).

None of these are unusual or dangerous for a healthy adult at normal amounts. The question isn't whether the ingredients are safe. It's whether they do what the marketing implies.

## The Big Claim: Can a Drink Lower Your BAC?

This is the heart of the product, so it deserves a careful answer.

### How your body actually clears alcohol

Almost all the alcohol you drink is broken down by your liver. An enzyme called **alcohol dehydrogenase** turns alcohol into a toxic compound called acetaldehyde, and a second enzyme, **aldehyde dehydrogenase**, turns acetaldehyde into harmless acetate. A small amount of alcohol also leaves through your breath, sweat, and urine, but that share is minor.

The key fact is that this system works at a **fairly fixed speed**. For most adults, BAC falls by roughly 0.015 percentage points per hour, which is about one standard drink per hour. That pace varies from person to person, and it can shift with genetics, body size, liver health, and how often you drink. But it doesn't respond much to anything you do in the moment. Coffee doesn't speed it up. Cold showers don't. Exercise doesn't in any useful way. Our guide on [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up) walks through the timeline in detail.

That's why every serious source on drunk driving says the same thing: **only time lowers your BAC.**

### What the research says about speeding it up

There is one small, real wrinkle in that rule, and it's probably the most generous scientific case anyone could make for a drink like Safety Shot.

**Fructose.** For decades, researchers have tested whether fructose (fruit sugar) can speed up alcohol elimination. Some older studies found a modest increase in how fast alcohol was cleared when people were given large amounts of fructose. Other studies found little or no effect, and the doses used were often large enough to cause stomach upset. The theory is that fructose helps the liver recycle a helper molecule (called NAD+) that alcohol dehydrogenase needs, letting the enzyme work a little faster. It's a genuine area of research, but the results are inconsistent, and nobody has shown it turns a dangerous BAC into a safe one.

**Food in general.** Eating a meal before or while drinking lowers your *peak* BAC, mostly because food slows how quickly alcohol moves from your stomach into your bloodstream. Some research also suggests a meal can modestly increase the elimination rate. This is one of the best-supported, most useful things you can do, and it's free.

**Vitamins and electrolytes.** There is no good evidence that B vitamins, vitamin C, or electrolytes lower BAC. They can matter for general health and hydration, but they don't make your liver process alcohol meaningfully faster.

So a drink containing sugars and nutrients might, in theory, nudge alcohol clearance slightly. "Slightly" is the important word. Even in the most favorable studies on fructose, the effect was nowhere near enough to change whether someone is safe to drive.

### What about the company's own studies?

Safety Shot's marketing has pointed to internal testing and to a patent as support for its claims. Two things are worth knowing:

1. **A patent is not proof that something works.** Patents protect an invention or formula. The patent office does not test whether a drink actually lowers BAC in people the way it's advertised.
2. **Company-run studies need outside checking.** Small studies run or funded by a company, especially ones not published in full in a peer-reviewed journal, can't be independently assessed. We don't know how many people were tested, how BAC was measured, whether there was a proper placebo comparison, or whether the results held up. Until that kind of data is published and repeated by independent researchers, the claim stays unproven.

We searched for independent, peer-reviewed research on Safety Shot specifically and did not find any. That doesn't prove the drink does nothing. It means there's no good evidence that it lowers BAC in a way that matters.

## Why You Should Never Drive on It

This is the most important section of this review.

### A lower number isn't the same as being sober

Even if a drink lowered your BAC a little, alcohol's effects on your brain don't line up neatly with a single number on a breathalyzer. Reaction time, judgment, coordination, and your ability to track several things at once all start to slip well before you reach the legal limit. Our guide to [what BAC means](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) explains how impairment builds as BAC rises.

People who believe they've taken something to "sober up" can also feel more confident than they should. That false confidence is exactly the wrong state of mind for driving.

### The legal limit is a ceiling, not a target

In most of the US, the legal limit for drivers 21 and older is 0.08% BAC, and it's lower in Utah (0.05%) and for commercial drivers. You can still be arrested and charged if you're impaired below the limit. Underage drivers face zero-tolerance rules in every state. See our guide to the [legal alcohol limit to drive](/never-hungover/legal-alcohol-limit-to-drive) for more.

None of these laws have an exception for drinks that claim to lower BAC, and "I drank a recovery shot" is not a defense.

### Timing makes it worse

Your BAC keeps rising for a while after your last drink, often for 30 to 90 minutes, as alcohol is still being absorbed from your stomach and gut. If you drink a recovery shot as you're leaving the bar and then drive, your BAC may actually be climbing during the drive, no matter what you just drank. Our guide on [how long after drinking you can drive](/never-hungover/how-long-after-drinking-can-you-drive) covers this in more detail.

### The plain rule

If you've had more than a small amount to drink, don't drive. Plan your ride before you start drinking. If you want a rough sense of where you might be, our [blood alcohol calculator](/never-hungover/blood-alcohol-calculator) can give you an estimate, but even it can't tell you you're safe to drive. Only a sober plan does that.

## Does Safety Shot Help With Hangovers?

This is a fairer question, and the answer is "maybe a little, for the same reasons most recovery drinks help a little."

A hangover is a mix of several things: dehydration, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, low-grade inflammation, a dip in blood sugar, and the after-effects of acetaldehyde. A drink with fluid, electrolytes, some sugar, and vitamins can address a few of those in a small way:

- **Fluid and electrolytes** can help if you're dehydrated. Water does much of this job too.
- **Sugar** can help if you feel shaky from low blood sugar.
- **B vitamins and vitamin C** are commonly included in hangover products. There's some research on vitamin levels and hangover severity, but there is no good evidence that taking them in a single drink makes a hangover much better.

What a drink like this can't do is fix poor sleep, undo stomach irritation, or reverse the main effects of a heavy night. If you feel better after drinking one, a good share of the credit probably goes to the fluid, the sugar, and time.

For a broader look at what tends to help, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Honest Pros and Cons

### Pros

- **Ingredients are familiar** and generally safe for healthy adults at normal amounts.
- **It adds fluid and electrolytes**, which can help with mild dehydration.
- **It's convenient**: ready to drink, no mixing.
- **It may contain sugar**, which can help if you feel shaky the morning after.

### Cons

- **The main marketing claim isn't backed by independent research.** We found no peer-reviewed trial showing it meaningfully lowers BAC.
- **It can create false confidence**, which is dangerous if anyone treats it as a reason to drive.
- **It tends to cost more** than water, an electrolyte packet, or a sports drink that does much of the same job.
- **The product has been rebranded and repositioned over time**, which makes it harder to know exactly what you're buying compared with older ads.
- **Sugar content may matter** to people managing their weight or blood sugar. Check the label.

## Who Should Be Careful

For most healthy adults, a single serving is unlikely to cause problems. Read the label and check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you:

- **Have diabetes or prediabetes**, since sugar content can affect blood sugar, and alcohol itself can cause blood sugar to drop.
- **Have kidney disease** or have been told to limit potassium, sodium, or other minerals.
- **Take prescription medicines**, especially for blood sugar, blood pressure, or mood. Many interact with alcohol on their own.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.**

There's also a less obvious risk. Anything sold as a way to "lower your BAC" can encourage people to drink more than they otherwise would, on the belief that they can undo it later. If you notice you're reaching for a product like this so you can drink more, that's a good moment to pause.

## How Safety Shot Compares to Other Options

People who search for Safety Shot are usually looking for one of two things: a way to sober up faster, or a way to feel better the next day. Here's how the main options stack up.

| Option | What it's for | Lowers BAC? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Safety Shot | Marketed as lowering BAC; recovery drink | No good evidence it does in a meaningful way | No independent peer-reviewed trials found |
| Time | Clearing alcohol | Yes, at roughly one drink per hour | Very well established |
| Eating a meal | Lowering peak BAC | Lowers the peak if eaten before or while drinking | Well established |
| Water and electrolytes | Rehydration | No | Helps with dehydration |
| ZBiotics | Breaking down acetaldehyde in the gut | No, and the brand doesn't claim it does | Limited independent human data |
| DHM supplements | Hangover support | No | Mostly animal and lab studies, limited human data |
| Coffee | Feeling more alert | No | Can mask drowsiness but doesn't lower BAC |

A few notes on this table:

- **ZBiotics** is an engineered probiotic that targets acetaldehyde, not alcohol, and it doesn't claim to lower BAC. Our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) goes through the evidence.
- **Coffee** can make a tired, drunk person feel more alert without making them less impaired, which can be its own kind of trap. See our guide to [coffee for a hangover](/never-hungover/coffee-for-hangover).
- If what you want is to speed things up, our guide on [how to speed up alcohol metabolism](/never-hungover/how-to-speed-up-alcohol-metabolism) explains what has evidence (very little) and what doesn't.

## Sobering-Up Myths Worth Dropping

Safety Shot entered a long tradition of products and tricks that promise to sober you up. None of these work the way people hope:

- **Coffee or energy drinks.** They can make you feel more awake, not less drunk.
- **Cold showers.** They can wake you up for a few minutes. Your BAC stays the same.
- **Throwing up.** It might remove alcohol still sitting in your stomach, but it doesn't lower what's already in your blood, and vomiting while very drunk can be dangerous.
- **Exercise or sweating it out.** The amount of alcohol that leaves through sweat and breath is too small to matter.
- **Breath mints or mouthwash before a breath test.** They don't lower BAC, and some mouthwashes contain alcohol.
- **"Sobering" drinks and pills.** We've found no product with good independent evidence that it meaningfully lowers BAC.

The only reliable method is time, and the only safe way home after drinking is one where you're not driving.

## What to Do Instead: A Simple Plan for a Night Out

If you want to feel better the next day and stay safe, these steps beat any shot:

1. **Plan your ride first.** Decide how you're getting home before you have your first drink.
2. **Eat a real meal** before or while you drink. It lowers your peak BAC.
3. **Pace yourself.** Roughly one standard drink per hour gives your liver a fighting chance.
4. **Alternate with water.** One glass of water between drinks helps with hydration and slows your pace.
5. **Have a glass of water and an electrolyte drink before bed.**
6. **Sleep as much as you can.** Poor sleep is a big part of how bad a hangover feels.

### Where DHM fits in

Some people add a supplement to that routine. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Most of the research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than proven. It's important to be clear: **DHM does not lower your BAC, it doesn't sober you up, and it doesn't make it safe to drive.** It's a possible hangover aid, nothing more.

If you want to try it, two well-reviewed options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). These are affiliate links, which means we earn a small commission if you buy, at no extra cost to you. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [honest look at whether DHM works](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) explains what the research does and doesn't show.

## The Bottom Line

- Safety Shot is a vitamin, electrolyte, and sugar drink marketed as lowering blood alcohol.
- There is no good evidence that it lowers BAC in a meaningful way. We found no independent, peer-reviewed trial of the product.
- The only small scientific hook is research on fructose and alcohol clearance, and those results are inconsistent and modest.
- It may help a little with mild dehydration the next day, like most recovery drinks.
- **Never drive after drinking because you had Safety Shot or any other "sobering" product.** Only time lowers your BAC, and your BAC can keep rising after your last drink.
- Plan your ride, eat, pace yourself, and drink water. Those habits do more than any shot.

For the broader question of whether any of these products deliver, see our look at [whether hangover pills actually work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-pills-actually-work).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Safety Shot actually lower your blood alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that it does in a meaningful way. The company has pointed to its own testing and a patent, but we could not find an independent, peer-reviewed trial showing Safety Shot lowers BAC in real drinkers. The only related research, on fructose speeding up alcohol clearance, has shown modest and inconsistent effects. Your liver clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, and nothing you drink changes that much.

**Can I drive after drinking Safety Shot?**

No. Safety Shot does not make it safe or legal to drive after drinking. Impairment starts below the legal limit, your BAC can keep rising for up to an hour or more after your last drink, and no state has an exception for drinks that claim to lower BAC. If you've been drinking, use a rideshare, a taxi, public transit, or a sober driver.

**Will Safety Shot help me pass a breathalyzer?**

There is no good evidence that it will. A breath test measures the alcohol in your blood through your breath, and only time reliably brings that down. Trying to beat a breath test is also a sign that you shouldn't be driving. Plan another way home.

**Does Safety Shot work for hangovers?**

It might help a little, mostly because it provides fluid, electrolytes, some sugar, and vitamins, like many recovery drinks. There is no good evidence that it prevents or cures hangovers. Water, an electrolyte drink, food, and sleep cover most of the same ground for less money.

**Is Safety Shot safe to drink?**

For most healthy adults, a single serving is unlikely to cause problems, since the ingredients are common vitamins, minerals, and sugars. Check the label and ask a doctor or pharmacist first if you have diabetes, kidney disease, take prescription medicines, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. The bigger safety risk is behavioral: treating it as a reason to drive or to drink more.

**What actually lowers your BAC faster?**

Nothing safely lowers it much faster than your body already does. Time is the only reliable method, at roughly one standard drink per hour. Eating a meal before or while drinking lowers your peak BAC, which is the most useful thing you can do. Coffee, cold showers, exercise, and "sobering" drinks don't meaningfully lower BAC.

**Is Safety Shot the same as DHM or ZBiotics?**

No. Safety Shot is marketed around lowering BAC. ZBiotics is an engineered probiotic that targets acetaldehyde in the gut and doesn't claim to lower BAC. DHM is a plant compound studied for hangover support, with mostly animal and lab research. None of the three lower BAC in a meaningful way, and none of them make it safe to drive.
